Chapter 219 0216 I Don't Want to Talk Anymore, I Have to Go to Class

On the fifth day of negotiations, the Carlyle Group, which had already left, was persuaded to return.

This was mainly because the other major venture capital firms had invested in too many projects over the past year. They needed a particularly well-funded peer to lead the investment!

Moreover, Carlyle sent a woman this time—Yang Lin, who had taken office at the end of last year as the Vice President for Asia (excluding Japan).

The reason Yang Lin came in person was that Facebook had completed its Series B financing. Its post-money valuation was $550 million!

The combined user base of the two websites under ByteDance (excluding overlapping users) far exceeded that of Facebook, and they possessed new features that Facebook lacked. In addition, there was also Kaixin Marketplace, as well as stakes in Tudou.com and Bailian Technology.

Yang Lin had analyzed the due diligence materials in detail and was very interested in ByteDance.

"With Carlyle leading this round, we only want one non-executive director seat," Yang Lin said. "I am also personally responsible for Carlyle's mergers and acquisitions and post-investment management in Asia (excluding Japan). If ByteDance has needs, I will personally help optimize the enterprise or help you acquire other companies. Especially for a future IPO, adjustments must be made to meet listing requirements."

Chen Guiliang smiled slightly. "Thank you very much. I need to add one independent director."

"Certainly," Yang Lin agreed without hesitation.

With this, the composition of ByteDance's board of directors would be as follows: 2 seats for the founder, 1 seat for the Series A lead investor (IDG), 1 seat for the Series B lead investor (Carlyle), and 1 seat for an independent director.

Chen Guiliang continued, "The candidate for the independent director must be nominated by me. When it comes to dismissing the independent director, I will have a veto vote."

The several venture capital managers exchanged glances.

The founder was being extremely assertive, but they had no choice but to accept.

This meant that only Chen Guiliang could propose candidates for the independent director. If he disagreed with dismissing the independent director, he could cast a veto vote.

Yang Lin asked, "Who do you plan to nominate as the independent director?"

Chen Guiliang said, "A professor of mine, Professor Wu, the Vice Dean of Peking University's Guanghua School of Management and founder of Peking University's Strategic Management Department."

"I agree," Yang Lin said.

"I agree as well."

The other investment managers nodded one after another.

An independent director could not be a current employee of the company, nor one who had left within the past year. They also could not have significant business dealings with the company, and certainly could not be a representative of an interested party (such as a relative).

Wang Kai, the incubation manager at Peking University Science Park, could have also served as an independent director.

But Wang Kai's reputation and position were not significant enough, and these investment firms might have been unwilling.

Bringing in Professor Wu was a perfect fit, and they could also leverage the resources at Professor Wu's disposal. At critical moments, Professor Wu would need to step in and help—giving him a tiny sliver of stock options would suffice.

Chen Guiliang produced another supplementary agreement. "I forgot about this during the Series A financing, so it's a good time to add it. I need to have a veto vote on board meeting agendas. The scope of this veto power applies to: amending the company's articles of association, financing and M&A, appointments and dismissals of senior executives, and business transformation."

Yang Lin was already at a loss for whether to laugh or cry. "Mr. Chen, you are very confident."

"Isn't a confident founder what venture capitalists like to see?" Chen Guiliang retorted.

Yang Lin said, "Let's stop here for this morning. We'll continue in the afternoon."

The Innovation Center of Peking University Science Park had already moved into a newly completed six-story building.

It was beautifully built, with a strong sense of architectural artistry.

"Whoa, Teacher Wang, this is a nice office," Chen Guiliang exclaimed as he entered.

Wang Kai laughed heartily. "I'm basking in your glory. I got promoted."

Wang Kai used to be just a Senior Incubation Manager. Last year, he was promoted to Deputy Director of the Incubation Services Department. His superior was also promoted this year, so Wang Kai took over and became the General Manager of the Incubation Department.

Although it had long since become corporatized and lacked clear administrative ranks, there was still a frame of reference. Wang Kai's current position was roughly equivalent to a Section Chief-level cadre within the university.

The rank was not high, but his actual authority was substantial!

Especially for the entrepreneurs among Peking University's faculty and students, they had to worship Wang Kai like a living Bodhisattva.

He really had basked in Chen Guiliang's glory, or else he wouldn't have been promoted so quickly.

Wang Kai personally brewed tea for Chen Guiliang, his face beaming with joy. "How are the Series B financing talks going? I heard you angered the Carlyle representative and made him leave a few days ago?"

"They came back, and this time it's Carlyle's Vice President for Asia." Chen Guiliang said.

Wang Kai was slightly surprised. "The Vice President for Asia is here to negotiate in person?"

Chen Guiliang speculated, "This VP is new, having just taken office at the end of last year. She probably wants to achieve something to solidify her position. I angered an investment manager, and she saw an opportunity to step in herself. Plus, I'm riding on Facebook's coattails."

"Facebook's Series B is also done?" Wang Kai asked.

Chen Guiliang nodded. "Post-money valuation of $550 million."

Wang Kai sucked in a sharp breath. "It's only been a little over half a year, and Facebook is already at $550 million? That's growing so fast!"

Chen Guiliang chuckled. "It's venture capital mania. Both the US and China have gone crazy."

In a few more months, Google would be the one to go truly crazy.

Just a year and a half after its creation, YouTube would be acquired by Google for a staggering $1.65 billion!

Once that deal was done, Tudou.com's value would also soar.

Inside a small conference room at the Peking University Science and Technology Building.

SoftBank's representative, Lin Heping, said, "This Chen Guiliang is just like Shanda's Chen Tianqiao and NetEase's Ding Sanshi, possessing a pathological desire for control over his company. As long as people like him don't make major erroneous decisions, they are actually excellent investment targets."

Yan Yan, the head of SoftBank China, hadn't come; he was busy leading investments in other companies.

This year, they had already invested in 58.com and were currently investing in Perfect World, Digital China, Mobi Antenna, and Eternal Asia... as well as making additional investments in PPTV and Acorn International.

So, SoftBank's presence at ByteDance this time was merely for a small follow-on investment; Carlyle was the lead investor.

DCM's venture partner, Feng Kaixuan, said, "Chen Guiliang's investment acumen is quite sharp. He's only made two investments, and both projects have soared. Bailian Technology and Tudou.com both have great potential."

IDG's Lin Dongliang smiled. "It doesn't matter to me. We and DJF already experienced this last year and were even forced to replace a director."

"Since no one has any objections, let's go for lunch first," Yang Lin said.

Yang Lin's family background was very mysterious and had never been disclosed publicly.

The outside world only knew that she graduated from Harvard with a double major. After graduation, she joined Tiger Asia Management, then moved to Goldman Sachs Investment Bank, and subsequently served as a director at KKR. Last year, she parachuted into Hong Kong to become the Vice President for Asia at Carlyle.

Many female investors who were thriving in China followed this career path.

Afternoon, the meeting continued.

Bailian Technology was valued at 500 million RMB (somewhat undervalued). ByteDance owned a 25% stake in it, which translated to 125 million RMB.

Tudou.com had recently completed its Series B financing with a post-money valuation of $40 million. ByteDance owned a 20% stake, which translated to $8 million.

Taking into account various factors like Xiaonei.com, Hainei.com (Kaixin.com), Kaixin Marketplace, Bailian Technology, and Tudou.com, ByteDance was valued at $150 million.
